Anyone can read the webview's bundle from the installed extension. Keep the key in the extension host, in `context.secrets` or the host's environment. + + +## How it works + +A webview has no server behind it. Its origin is `vscode-webview://`, its Content Security Policy only allows resources from the extension, and a relative `fetch("/api/chat")` reaches nothing. `@assistant-ui/vscode` tunnels `fetch` over the webview's `postMessage` channel instead. + +```mermaid +flowchart LR + Webview["Webview
assistant-ui React"] -->|"vscodeFetch"| Channel["postMessage"] + Channel --> Host["Extension host
serveWebviewHost"] + Host -->|"Request"| Route["POST(req) route handler"] + Route --> Provider["Model or agent"] +``` + +- In the webview, `vscodeFetch` has the signature of `fetch`. It sends the request over the channel and returns a `Response` whose body streams as the host writes it. +- In the extension host, `serveWebviewHost` rebuilds a standard `Request`, calls the route handler for its path and method, and streams the `Response` back. Stopping a run in the webview aborts `req.signal` in the handler, and so does reloading the webview: the new page tells the host to abort the requests the old page left running. + +The extension host runs Node.js, which has the web `Request` and `Response` classes. The `dev` task builds the extension in watch mode, and an Extension Development Host window opens with the **Assistant** view in the secondary side bar. The first time the view opens, it prompts you to set your OpenAI API key, which it stores in VS Code's secret storage. Run **Assistant: Set OpenAI API Key** from the Command Palette to change it. + +| File | Runs in | Contents | +| --- | --- | --- | +| `src/extension.ts` | Extension host | Registers the webview view, serves its routes, and writes its HTML | +| `src/api/chat/route.ts` | Extension host | The AI SDK chat route, the same handler as in the Next.js `default` template | +| `src/webview/assistant.tsx` | Webview | `useChatRuntime` over `vscodeFetch`, and the `Thread` component | +| `src/webview/app.css` | Webview | Tailwind and the VS Code theme | +| `scripts/build.mts` | Build | esbuild for the host and the webview, and Tailwind for the CSS | + +`npm run package` builds a `.vsix` with `@vscode/vsce` once you set your `publisher` in `package.json`. + +## Add to an existing extension + +### 1. + +
+ + ); +}; + +const root = document.getElementById("root"); +if (root) createRoot(root).render(); +``` + +`sendAutomaticallyWhen` continues the run after a frontend tool, such as an approval, adds its result. + +### 4. Bundle both sides + +The extension host loads a CommonJS bundle that leaves `vscode` external. The template's build script also runs Tailwind for `app.css` and has a watch mode for F5. + +A single bundle also inlines everything a component can load lazily. The Shiki highlighter is the large case: it loads each grammar on demand, so a single bundle carries every grammar and theme, about 15 MB. To keep the webview small, pass a `highlighter` built with only the languages you need, or build the webview as ESM with code splitting and keep `renderWebviewHtml`'s default module script type. A module script's imports, `import()` included, inherit its nonce, so the chunks load without a `scriptSrc` entry.
comment.body: the guide qualifies this now instead of adding a probe: it says chunks "should load" without a `scriptSrc` entry, notes that the VS Code test bed only runs a single bundle, and tells readers to check **Developer: Open Webview Developer Tools** for CSP errors after switching to code splitting ([vscode.mdx#L211](https://github.com/assistant-ui/assistant-ui/blob/bnb/vscode-publish/apps/docs/content/docs/guides/vscode.mdx#L211)). a split-bundle probe would need a second webview build in the example, which is more than this PR should carry.

comment.body: fixed in e03e19c31: step 1 now installs `react` and `react-dom`, plus `@types/react` and `@types/react-dom` as dev dependencies. `@assistant-ui/react` only lists the types as optional peers, so npm skipped them and the sample didn't typecheck in a fresh extension.

Keeping `@types/react` as a required peer. I packed the package and type-checked a clean npm consumer against each entry point (TypeScript 7, `skipLibCheck: false`):

| Consumer | `@types/react` installed | Errors |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@assistant-ui/vscode/host` only | no | 0 |
| `@assistant-ui/vscode/webview` only | no | 56, all in `@assistant-ui/core/dist/react/*.d.ts` |
| both entries | yes, npm installs the required peer | 0 |

You're right about the host entry: its program loads no `@assistant-ui/core` or React declarations at all. The webview entry does, because `createVSCodeStorage` returns `AsyncStorageLike` from `@assistant-ui/core/react` ([`storage.ts#L1`](https://github.com/assistant-ui/assistant-ui/blob/7d352ecdf93b8510cffafe541776345757e5552c/packages/vscode/src/webview/storage.ts#L1)). Both entries ship in one package, so with an optional peer a webview consumer without React's types gets those 56 errors, which is the same failure #8846 fixed for `@assistant-ui/vue`. For a host-only consumer the required peer costs a types-only package that npm and pnpm install on their own and that its program never reads. Moving from required to optional later doesn't break anyone, and the reverse would, so I'd rather publish it required.

issue.title: ci(docs): check docs links weekly and on demand

labels.name: stage/ready
labels.description: Approved with passing CI; ready to merge

labels.name: tier/3
labels.description: Review tier T3, set by the review-tier check

issue.body: Part of #10292 ## Problem Nothing checks the docs for broken links, so they land unnoticed. A crawl of main found six. ## Change Adds linkinator with apps/docs/linkinator.config.mjs and a check:links turbo task that builds the docs, serves the production build on port 3331 with start-server-and-test, and crawls it. The crawl starts from the sitemap, because the docs sidebar renders on the client, and rewrites absolute production URLs to the local build so those paths are checked against the commit under test. Local runs check internal links only. The workflow sets LINKINATOR_EXTERNAL=1 to add external links, at concurrency 10 with a 20 second timeout and retries. Both modes skip /packages and /traction, which call the npm and GitHub APIs on every request. The external run also skips localhost links in quickstarts, this repository's generated commit, pull request, release and edit links, and medium.com, which answers 403 to non-browser clients. The config comments give the reason for each. Adds .github/workflows/linkinator.yaml. It runs weekly (Mondays at 05:41 UTC) and on workflow_dispatch, not on pull requests, because it builds the whole docs site. Setup matches the neighbouring workflows: pnpm/setup, ubuntu-latest, SHA pins with ratchet comments. Every scheduled run calls the new reusable .github/workflows/scheduled-failure-issue.yaml from a report job. A failure comments on the open issue with the same title or opens one, and a pass closes that issue. That job is the only one with issues: write. CONTRIBUTING.md documents the local command. Left out: running this on pull requests. Because the workflow is new and has no pull_request trigger, it cannot run on this pull request. The first real run is a dispatch after merge. This fails on main until the pull request that fixes the six links lands, so that one should merge first. ## Verification All on a production build of 3fa379f81, on a Mac, with the 1-minute load average between 20 and 80: - `pnpm turbo run check:links --filter=@assistant-ui/docs-site`: 3241 links, 2 broken, exit 1. One is the harnesses link. The other, /media/c-major-arpeggio.mp3, returned status 0 in that run only: the file serves 200 on its own and passed in the two later full crawls. - `LINKINATOR_EXTERNAL=1 pnpm turbo run check:links --filter=@assistant-ui/docs-site`: 3607 links, 6 broken, exit 1. - The same command with the link fixes applied: 3603 links, 0 broken, exit 0. - `actionlint` is clean on both workflow files. `zizmor --offline` reports one low finding, self-repository, on the `uses: ./` reference to the reusable workflow. - `pnpm lint` and `pnpm knip:check` pass. ## Decision T3, because the report job has issues: write. #10292 ## Public surface None. apps/docs is private. ## AI use Claude Code wrote these changes and ran the commands listed under Verification.

comment.body:
@rupic-app the open findings in this summary are settled or are gates only a maintainer can clear:

- Decision: the body now links #10292 in place of `#AUI_DECISION_ISSUE`. The issue still needs its accepted decision.
- Size: `pnpm-lock.yaml` is listed in `generatedPaths` in [`.github/review-policy.json#L85`](https://github.com/assistant-ui/assistant-ui/blob/5d55d7eb66e41e859baf2994c141693cef28f466/.github/review-policy.json#L85), and the 400-line cap skips generated files ([`CONTRIBUTING.md#L83`](https://github.com/assistant-ui/assistant-ui/blob/5d55d7eb66e41e859baf2994c141693cef28f466/CONTRIBUTING.md#L83)). Outside tests, generated files and T0 paths, this PR changes 119 lines, and the review-tier comment raises no size signal.
- The four outdated review threads are resolved.

On the second issue reporter: `react18-weekly.yaml` keeps its inline reporter in this PR. Moving it onto `scheduled-failure-issue.yaml` changes a workflow this PR doesn't otherwise touch, so it belongs in its own follow-up.

I also merged main into the branch. It merged cleanly, the lockfile installs with `--frozen-lockfile`, and since main moved the docs off fumadocs-mdx I ran `check:links` locally on the merged branch: the docs built, and linkinator scanned 3279 internal links with no failures.

issue.body: Part of #10292 ## Problem Nothing measures the docs site's performance, accessibility, best practices or SEO, so regressions land unnoticed. ## Change Adds Lighthouse CI (@lhci/cli) with apps/docs/lighthouserc.yml and a check:lighthouse turbo task that builds the docs and runs lhci autorun. lhci starts the production build on port 3332 and audits three pages three times each: the home page, /docs/runtimes/ai-sdk/overview and /playground. Each category is checked on the median of the three runs, per page. @lhci/cli 0.15.1, the latest release, bundles Lighthouse 12.6.1, which returned no performance score (NO_LCP) on current Chrome, so pnpm-workspace.yaml overrides lighthouse to ^13.5.0. It resolves to 13.6.0, and @opentelemetry/instrumentation stays at 0.223.0 in the lockfile. Reports are written with the filesystem upload target and uploaded as the lighthouse-reports workflow artifact for 14 days. Nothing goes to temporary public storage. Adds .github/workflows/lighthouse.yaml. It runs weekly (Mondays at 06:17 UTC) and on workflow_dispatch, not on pull requests, because it builds the whole docs site. Setup matches the neighbouring workflows: pnpm/setup, ubuntu-latest, SHA pins with ratchet comments. Every scheduled run calls the reusable .github/workflows/scheduled-failure-issue.yaml from a report job. A failure comments on the open issue with the same title or opens one, and a pass closes that issue. That job is the only one with issues: write. The file is identical to the one in the link check pull request. Adds .lighthouseci to the docs .gitignore and the local command to CONTRIBUTING.md. Left out: fixes for the accessibility findings, desktop-preset audits, and running this on pull requests. Because the workflow is new and has no pull_request trigger, it cannot run on this pull request. The first real run is a dispatch after merge, and it will show whether the performance floors suit GitHub's runners. ## Verification `pnpm turbo run check:lighthouse --filter=@assistant-ui/docs-site` on a production build of 3fa379f81 exits 0, with Lighthouse 13.6.0 and the 1-minute load average between 21 and 81, so the performance figures are pessimistic and not final. Scores across the three runs per page: - Home: performance 0.76 to 0.86, accessibility 0.77, best practices 0.92, SEO 1. - Docs page: performance 0.78 to 0.86, accessibility 0.91, best practices 0.92, SEO 1. - Playground: performance 0.63 to 0.70, accessibility 0.88, best practices 0.92, SEO 1. The floors in lighthouserc.yml are unchanged from earlier measurements (performance 0.55 to 0.6), which were also taken under load. Accessibility, best practices and SEO scores matched in every run and clear their floors by 0.01. `actionlint` is clean on both workflow files, `zizmor --offline` reports one low finding, self-repository, on the `uses: ./` reference. `pnpm lint` and `pnpm knip:check` pass. ## Decision T3, because the report job has issues: write. #10292 ## Public surface None. apps/docs is private. ## AI use Claude Code wrote these changes and ran the commands listed under Verification.

comment.body:
Fixed in 5e036fab7. The advice was wrong in two ways:

- `scriptSrc` entries go through `sources()` ([`html.ts#L74-L83`](https://github.com/assistant-ui/assistant-ui/blob/7d352ecdf93b8510cffafe541776345757e5552c/packages/vscode/src/host/html.ts#L74-L83)), which rejects whitespace and quotes ([`#L55`](https://github.com/assistant-ui/assistant-ui/blob/7d352ecdf93b8510cffafe541776345757e5552c/packages/vscode/src/host/html.ts#L55)). Against the built package, `scriptSrc: [webview.cspSource]` throws `Invalid script-src source: "'self' https://*.vscode-cdn.net". Pass one host or scheme source per entry.` Extra sources take no keywords on purpose (the test at [`html.test.ts#L129`](https://github.com/assistant-ui/assistant-ui/blob/7d352ecdf93b8510cffafe541776345757e5552c/packages/vscode/src/host/html.test.ts#L129) requires `frameSrc: ["'self'"]` to throw), so I left the validation alone.
- The chunks never needed an entry. A module script's imports, `import()` included, are fetched with the importing script's nonce ([descendant script fetch options](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#descendant-script-fetch-options)). In headless Chromium 156, a nonced module script on a page with `default-src 'none'; script-src 'nonce-abc'` loaded both a static and an `import()` chunk, and a `<script type="module">` added without the nonce was blocked.

The commit removes the advice from the guide, the README and the `scriptSrc` doc comment, notes that each extra source takes one host or scheme, and adds a test that a source list passed as one `scriptSrc` entry throws. The guide line now reads:

```suggestion
A single bundle also inlines everything a component can load lazily. The Shiki highlighter is the large case: it loads each grammar on demand, so a single bundle carries every grammar and theme, about 15 MB. To keep the webview small, pass a `highlighter` built with only the languages you need, or build the webview as ESM with code splitting and keep `renderWebviewHtml`'s default module script type. A module script's imports, `import()` included, inherit its nonce, so the chunks load without a `scriptSrc` entry.
```

issue.title: chore: run the user's global git hooks from husky

labels.name: stage/needs-review
labels.description: No reviews yet; waiting for a maintainer

issue.body: ## Summary Husky only runs a hook, and `~/.config/husky/init.sh` with it, when `.husky/` exists in the checkout. This repo tracked only `pre-commit`, so `prepare-commit-msg` and `pre-push` never ran in a fresh clone or a worktree. With tracehub, that meant commits got no `Assisted-by` trailer and pushes uploaded no trace. Added `.husky/global-hook`, copied from assistant-ui/assistant-ui#10153. It runs a global `core.hooksPath` hook that husky's own `core.hooksPath` would otherwise shadow. Added `.husky/pre-push` and `.husky/prepare-commit-msg`, each a single line that sources it. Nothing else changed. ## Type - [ ] Model data fix (correcting wrong values) - [ ] New model or provider - [ ] Fetch script improvement - [ ] Bug fix - [ ] Feature - [x] Other ## Source Not a data change. ## Checklist - [ ] `pnpm validate` passes (for data changes) - [x] `pnpm lint` passes - [ ] Data changes include a source link Unlike assistant-ui/assistant-ui#10153, `global-hook` passes `--includes` to its `git config` lookups, so a hooks path set inside an include or includeIf file is found too.

comment.body:
@rupic-app on the test note: the husky hooks aren't under a test suite here, so I checked the helper by hand in a scratch repo with `core.hooksPath` set only through an `[include]`. The global hook ran before the repo hook, a global hook exiting 3 made `.husky/pre-commit` exit 3 without running the rest, and with `--includes` removed the global hook never ran.

Also, [0ba80bb](https://github.com/assistant-ui/modelpedia/pull/186/commits/0ba80bb38eb5499c019d592574bb7755d4ab025d) makes `.husky/pre-commit` source `global-hook` too, so a global pre-commit hook runs like the other two, the same way [assistant-ui#10153](https://github.com/assistant-ui/assistant-ui/pull/10153) does it.

issue.title: feat(vscode): publish @assistant-ui/vscode to npm
issue.body: ### Problem `@assistant-ui/vscode` landed private in #8690: `packages/vscode/package.json` is `"private": true` at `0.0.0`, and `npm view @assistant-ui/vscode` answers `E404`. A VS Code extension outside this repository therefore cannot use it, and the only consumers are `examples/with-vscode` and `templates/vscode`, which take it from the workspace. The `vscode` template cannot be offered by `create` either. The CLI rewrites the template's `workspace:*` dependencies to `latest`, so a scaffolded project would ask npm for a package that does not exist. Since #8690 the package has had the reload cancellation fix (#9096) and a VS Code test bed that runs on every change to the package (`vscode-test-bed.yaml`, VS Code 1.140.0), so the surface has been exercised against a real webview. ### Where packages/vscode, packages/cli (`create` template list), packages/create-assistant-ui (README), templates/vscode, apps/docs (VS Code guide, packages list), api-surface, .changeset ### Found via Follow-up to #8690. `packages/AGENTS.md` keeps a new package private until it publishes, and #9254 (variants) and #8841 (vue) are the publish precedents. ### Proposed change Publish the package under its current name, `@assistant-ui/vscode`, with the surface it has on main today: - `@assistant-ui/vscode/webview`: `vscodeFetch`, `createVSCodeFetch`, `installLinkInterceptor`, `createVSCodeStorage`, `getVSCodeApi`, `getCspNonce` - `@assistant-ui/vscode/host`: `serveWebviewHost`, `serveWebviewRoutes`, `renderWebviewHtml`, `createWebviewCsp`, `createCspNonce` - `@assistant-ui/vscode/theme.css` - both entries also export the bridge protocol types and guards from `protocol.ts` The publish pull request: - drops `private` and adds `publishConfig` (`access: public`, `provenance: true`), with a `patch` changeset so the first release is `0.0.1` - adds the `api-surface/` snapshot, the packages page entry that `traction-packages.test.ts` requires, a Guides > Environments page, and an npm install line in the README - registers `vscode` in `create`, printing `code .` and "press F5" as the next steps, with a `patch` changeset for `assistant-ui` - keeps `@assistant-ui/core` as a caret dependency and `react` as an optional peer, and makes `@types/react` a required peer: the webview declarations import `AsyncStorageLike` from `@assistant-ui/core/react`, so a clean consumer with `skipLibCheck: false` and no `@types/react` reports 50 TS7016 errors, the case #8846 fixed for Vue - writes up what the webview can ask of the extension host and the reverse One fix lands separately before the publish pull request: #HOST_ORIGIN has the host refuse a request for an `http:` or `https:` origin other than the bridge's own, which today only `vscodeFetch` refuses, and tests the message fields the bridge validates. Before the release runs, a maintainer publishes a placeholder and sets up trusted publishing by hand, since `npm trust` answers `E404` for a name that has never published (#9257). This adds a new public package and a new `create` template and changes `api-surface/`, so it is T3 under the review policy and needs a `decision: accepted` label from an owner of the Public API area. ### Done when `@assistant-ui/vscode@0.0.1` is on npm with provenance from `npm-publish.yaml`, `npx assistant-ui@latest create my-extension -t vscode` scaffolds a project that installs, typechecks and builds, and the VS Code guide is live on the docs site.

issue.title: ci(docs): check the docs site's Lighthouse scores and links every week
issue.body: ### Problem Nothing measures the docs site's Lighthouse scores or checks its links, so slower pages, accessibility regressions and broken links land unnoticed. A crawl of main found six broken links, fixed in #10239. ### Where .github/workflows (new `lighthouse.yaml`, `linkinator.yaml` and the reusable `scheduled-failure-issue.yaml`), apps/docs, CONTRIBUTING.md ### Found via A crawl of main while fixing the docs links in #10239. ### Proposed change Two workflows that build the docs and check the production build, weekly and on `workflow_dispatch`. Neither runs on pull requests, since each builds the whole site. - Lighthouse CI audits the home page, an AI SDK docs page and /playground three times each and checks every category on the median. Reports are kept as a workflow artifact for 14 days. (#10240) - linkinator crawls from the sitemap: internal links locally, and external links as well in CI. (#10241) Each scheduled run reports through `scheduled-failure-issue.yaml`: a failure comments on the open issue with the workflow's title or opens one, and a pass closes it. That report job is the only one with `issues: write`. This adds workflows with a schedule trigger and an `issues: write` job, so it is T3 under the review policy and needs a `decision: accepted` label from an owner. ### Done when Both workflows are on main, a dispatched run of each has passed or opened its tracking issue, and the Lighthouse floors are set from that first run on GitHub's runners.

issue.title: Proposal: Kit, doc-kit's mascot, and a tagline for the site
issue.body: Hey folks 👋 On #1192 we agreed the branding needs its own discussion, so here's a proposal for it. The PR uses all of this for now, and I'm happy to swap any of it for whatever we land on here. ## Kit A cat called Kit, after doc-kit. It's a flat head, so it works as a mark from a 16px favicon up to the home page's hero, in both color schemes, and it has a couple of poses for the spots where the site can be a bit playful: asleep on the 404 page, and peeking over the home page's last section. On the PR the drawings live in `www/theme/components/Brand.jsx` and `www/public/`. ## Tagline The home page's headline is a placeholder for now, "The docs toolkit for APIs." A few other ideas: - The docs toolkit for APIs. - API docs from plain Markdown. - Write it once, get every format. - The toolkit behind the Node.js API docs. ## Colors The site sticks to the neutral greys doc-kit's default theme already uses, no green, so it doesn't read as a Node.js page out of the box. What do y'all think? cc @avivkeller

comment.body: I know I was/am extremely critical of the Node.js mascot, I want to also make sure to give feedback when my opinion is positive: this is great, I love this mascot _a lot_.
